Mr. W. H. BENNETT (East Simcoe) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 50, to amend the Insurance Act, 1910.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this Bill is in the same terms as a certain Bill which was introduced by the late Mr. Lancaster, member for Lincoln, three or four years ago. The purport of the Bill is this: Certain insurance companies have coalesced with other insurance companies, not only in Ontario but in other parts of the Dominion, and certain companies which have absorbed smaller companies have introduced terms into their policies which were not consonant with the terms that were in the policies of the companies whose affairs were taken over. That, at least, is the contention of those who are interested in one particular insurance company, the name of which I need not at present mention, as that will develop when the case is under consideration in the committee. In view of the fact that the Minister of Finance also has a Bill on the Order Paper for reference to the Insurance Committee, I would ask that this Bill be allowed to go to that committee, where the whole matter can be further discussed by the parties interested.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

1.	Have any assurances of exemption from Military Service been given by the Government of Canada to immigrants?
2.	If so, what are these assurances?

1 and 2. On account of representations made in the United States that immigrants to Canada were likely to be at once drafted for overseas military service, the Minister of the Interior, under date of January 8, 1916, addressed a general letter to the press of the United States, reading in part as follows :
"I, therefore, beg to advise you that all troops from Canada for the war have gone voluntarily; that while the Government has the power to enforce conscription, such action has not been considered, either advisable or necessary, and that even were conscription introduced it would apply to Canadian citizens only."
Those from the United States not British subjects nor alien enemies, entering Canada this year in response to the appeal for farm help in the Western Provinces, were furnished upon request with a certificate which stated that while they retained their present citizenship, they would not be called upon for military service. Since the United States entered the war the issue of this certificate has been discontinued, as has all advertising referring to the fact that there is no conscription in Canada. The members of any religious1 sect, such as the Society of Quakers, Mennonites, Tunkers or Doukhobors, who, on account of their

doctrines of religious belief, are averse to bearing arms, have been given assurance that upon coming to Canada they shall be exempt from military service, in accordance with the existing legislation in this respect.

1, 2, 3, 4. Silk velvets and silk cloths are subject to customs duties on importation into Canada. The additions to the invoice values thereof by the collector of customs or appraisers vary in amount;-but are made for the protection of the revenue under the provisions of Section 43, Customs Act, which require the collector, or appraiser, as the case may be, to estimate and appraise the true and fair market value

(any invoice or affidavit thereto to the contrary notwithstanding) of the goods at the time of their exportation to Canada.
The first appraisements are open to appeal, and are usually adjusted by reappraisement or production of other invoices so that if excess duties have been collected they are refunded.

MOTION BY Mr. CURRIE, M. P.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. CURRIE (North Simcoe) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, with a view to increasing the power of the Allies in the prosecution of the war, the Government should enter into immediate consultation with His Majesty's Governments in Great Britain, the other Dominions, India and the Colonies, in order, with their aid, to bring the whole economic strength of the Empire into co-operation with our Allies in a policy directed against the enemy.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion, which appears on the Order Paper, has been there for some time. It is almost similar in character to a motion that was passed unanimously by the British House of Commons on January 10 of last year. Since that motion was adopted in the British House of Commons, we have had a number of commissions and boards of inquiry dealing with matters appertaining to the subject which may properly come under the heading of this motion. In Great Britain
m

we have had the Economic Congress at Paris which discussed matters coming under the heading of this resolution. We have also had Lord Farrington's commission ,oh banking, which dealt with foreign banking. We have had the Royal Commission on Transportation, which dealt with transportation between the colonies and Great Britain, and also between Great Britain and foreign countries. Then we have had the recent commission to Washington, which dealt with matters pertaining to the war. We have had perhaps the most important commission of all the gatherings of imperial commissioners at London recently, a conference in which our own ministers took part; and no doubt we shall shortly have a report from that commission or conference laid before this 'House. Thus the motion might to some extent be considered superfluous, so far as discussion in this House is concerned, but as long as the war continues matters will continually arise pertaining to this question, and I think it would perhaps be just as well for the House to affirm its position in the matter of the war and ,our relations to the Allies. In the first place, I think it is advisable that we should affirm our position so far as our own people are concerned, and state to them clearly that this House and this country have a definite economic objective not only during, hut after the war, that we intend to do something after the war. The people of this country must not consider that this Parliament is carrying on this war in a lackadaisical way or has neglected to take into consideration question of economics that may arise not only during the war but after it. In the second place, it is important to define our position towards the Allies. The Allies have an economic position as well as a position in the war. We have given them an assurance that we are with them so far as men and munitions are concerned, and we have granted aid in the way of money to assist the Allies in the war. We should define our position to some extent, and say that it is our intention to carry on a vigorous policy to the conclusion of the war, until we have an honourable peace. In the third place, it is as well for us as a House to make it plain that we are prepared to support the men we now have in' the field and that this House is with them heart and soul, and is prepared to support them on every occasion. They must know that we have not sent them to the war to waste away and fritter their strength needlessly and without support-,
but that it is our intention to carry on the war vigorously, to raise further troops, to feed them and clothe them and support them in every possible way.
I should like the House to discuss this question without any partisan spirit. The resolution which appeared on the English order paper was in similar words and was discussed by both sides of that House and passed unanimously. I hope that the same measure of treatment will be accorded to this resolution, because I think that, taking all together, for the past year or year and a half we_ have had a little bit too much politics in this' country. We have 'been carrying on under a supposed flag of truce, and at the same time carry on Prussian politice-that is shooting from under a white flag. I think it is a great mistake for this country and for the members of this House to take part in any political fights outside of this House or to participate in partisan discussions of any kind when matters are at such a critical stage. It is quite true that until a few months ago the full strength of the enemy was not realized; but anybody who reads the terrible lists of casualties that fill the columns of our papers every day and who -remembers the fact that we have lost 25,000 men this year, that one whole division has been wiped out and that there has as yet been no definite issue to the war, must realize that this is no time for carrying on partisan warfare. We should settle down to business and united carry on the business of the country, supporting any measures that may come before the House affecting the war. Unless we win this war the loss to this country will be far greater than to any of the Allies or any of the other nations that are involved in it.
What is the position of Canada so far as this war is concerned? Canada is the only country or the only Dominion that has gone into this war without the hope of receiving anything from it. Let us look at the position of the Allies. Russia expects or expected to derive large acquisitions of territory. She looked forward to the time when she would receive Constantinople, supposed, in the language of Napoleon, to he the heart of the world. It has been the earnest hope of the Russians for centuries that the day would come when the Christian flag would fly over the great Church of St. Sophia and when the Holy Land would be under the dominion, possibly of the Czar, at least of a Christian nation.
Italy expects large accessions of territory, not only in Austria, but in Asia Minor. It

speechtext: I think the hon. member should be allowed considerable latitude in discussing an economic question of this kind.
Go on with your partisan speech.

I have not filled Hansard up this session with speeches like the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) has done. I shall endeavour to curtail my remarks to the subject of the resolution, and if hon. gentlemen object that I am wandering slightly afield I think it will be rather because I am treading a little too hard on their corns. I think it is extremely important for this country to discuss its economic position both now and after the war. Unless wp consider now

what our economic position will be after the war, when hon. gentlemen opposite come into power, as they expect to do, what will they find? Will they find this country in bankruptcy, a broken country without business or population? That is apparently the doctrine that some hon. gentlemen opposite have been preaching. I have been endeavouring to show that the policy which has been adopted by the Conservative party since 1878 is the proper economic policy for this country. I think under that poliey we shall be able to build up and make our country great after the war. If we want to get population into this country, it is just as important for us to get industrial workers as it is to get farmers. We must work out our own salvation. I am not one of those who are constantly looking for handouts from the United States or some other country. This country should be independent and carry on its business affairs with a view to the future regardless entirely of what any other country may do. Sir John A. Macdonald, one of the great leaders in this country, laid it down distinctly as part of his policy that he would let no other country interfere with the economic policy of Canada, and not so very many years ago the Canadian people endorsed that principle as the right hon. leader of the Opposition knows.
No, no.

The people in 1911 said they were not going to allow this country to be tangled up with the economic policy of any other country. Sad to say, that is when the right hon. gentleman failed. If we are to develop our full economic strength, not only during the war but after the war, we must carry on the same line of policy that we are now carrying on. That is the policy that has made a great industrial Germany; it is the same policy as that which has made the United States such a great country.
What, then, are we to do? We have here great resources. One thing that is fundamentally necessary is that we should encourage agriculture. Agriculture is one of our basic industries. It has been treated too much as an accident, and not as a technical trade. Any man is supposed to be good enough to be a farmer. We laugh and sneer at the Huns, the terrible Huns. But Hungary is far ahead of this country in its agricultural progress. There is not one of these central states of Europe, with which we are at war, but has a great system of agricultural colleges and high schools. Hun-

gary, for instance, has thirty-five agricultural high schools. Our agricultural development must be directed along the same lines. At present it costs us far too much to produce the things that are sold from our farms. We must develop our agriculture on technical lines.
We must develop our mines. We know that we have vast mineral resources, but what they are we are only discovering from day to day. After the war we should have thousands of men employed in our mines, not only our gold and silver mines, but our great coal-fields of the West. There are enormous coal areas in Alberta into which a pick has never been struck, as well as great areas of iron. I have no doubt that there are men now within the sound of my voice who will live to see Edmonton the Pittsburg of this country. At present, none of these mines are developed. Why should we go on simply growing and shipping wheat and pay so little attention to our mines? We must have population; we must have a mixed population; and in order to give employment to all classes we must have various industries developed.
Then, consider our forests. We have vast areas suitable for the production of pulp, and the pulp industry has received a great impetus within the last few years. At the time when the war broke out, Germany controlled almost entirely the printing and lithographing trade of Europe. Many thousands of people were employed in those trades-in one city no less than 15,000 people gained their livelihood in these industries. If Canada can produce paper more cheaply than any other country, why should we not become the centre of the lithographing and printing industries of the world? I am sure that every member of this House would gladly see such a state of affairs 4 p.m. brought about, but you cannot do that if you discourage our manufacturing industries. It is too much the habit of some people to find fault with our manufacturers. Take, for instance, our textile industries. They were starved for years because there was always a politician to raise a yell whenever somebody thought the woollen factories were making too much money. We have not developed the sheep industry and the production of wool as we ought to have done, and just for the same reason. Politics have been the curse of this country in many cases-
Hear, hear.

-and the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) knows that to
be the case. If he had his own way there are many things he would not stand for that he does stand for now, many policies that his followers promote, which, if he expressed his own ideas, he would oppose.
Our fisheries offer great opportunities. They have not been developed as the fisheries have been developed in Great Britain. With the coming of the trawler the development of our fisheries will mean many millions added to the wealth of this country, and a great population carrying on this industry.
It is not necessary for me to go through the whole list of our industries. But there is one thing most important of all, which must not be forgotten, and that is our foreign trade. Only a few months before the United States entered the war-and I am sure we all welcome the accession of the United States in this war, as bringing about once more a great Anglo-Saxon union-an economic conference was held by the manufacturers of that country. I take the trade papers, and had the pleasure of reading the discussions of that conference. It was pointed out that it would be the duty of the United States, after the war, to organize their industries for the carrying on of a more extensive foreign trade than that which they now enjoy. The expansion of the United States up to this time has been such as to absorb almost entirely the manufactures of that country. But they look forvjard to supplying foreign countries after the war is over. The manufacturers of the United States made a careful inquiry into the question how they could carry on business with various foreign countries- how they could extend their trade with South America, how ,they could increase their dealings with Russia, and so on. They discovered that if they were to compete with the Central European powers in this trade, one thing the country would have to do would be to organize foreign banking so that they could afford the long-term credits that these countries require. They found also that it would be necessary to obliterate some of the legislation that had been placed on their statute books with reference to trusts, because the manufacturers in allied industries would have to combine for the purposes of foreign trade. They found also that it would be necessary to follow the example of the Germans in pooling freights, so as to put the manufacturers in different centres upon an equal footing in relation to foreign business. In Germany manufacturers before the war, were given the same advantage in freights

whether their goods were produced in Dresden or in Hamburg. The railways and steamers absorbed the difference. What does that mean for us? It means that before the war ends our manufacturers must get together, and the country must cooperate with them, in order that means may be devised whereby our banking system will be extended to those foreign countries in which we hope to find markets. It means also that our manufacturers must be prepared to form unions, or committees, or commissions, to promote the sale of their products in foreign countries. And, if we are going to take over our railways-and we shall take them over or do something else with them-such arrangements must be made that the manufacturer at Winnipeg will have the same advantage in relation to foreign trade as the manufacturer at Toronto or Montreal. Then we shall be able to have great cities in these vast agricultural areas of the West, and the country will grow as it should. Otherwise, manufacturing in the West will be impossible, and the result will be disastrous to the country. Our industries will not grow as they should, and we shall not be able to pay off the great public debt we are taking on our shoulders.
Another thing to be dealt with is shipbuilding and our navigation laws. Shipbuilding is a problem that should receive our most earnest attention. Japan, for instance, by adopting a forward policy in shipbuilding and in shipping, succeeded in a few years in capturing all the Oriental trade. They built their ships and were able to take the trade from Great Britain, from the United States, and even from Germany, so far as the Pacific is concerned. The present moment is a very, critical one for this country. We must endeavour to stimulate shipbuilding, including wooden shipbuilding. A wooden ship will last for fifteen years. There is still plenty of timber in Canada. It is a great pleasure to me to know that the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) has seen fit to hand over money to the Imperial Munitions Board for the building of ships in Canada. What is more, I hope that some laws may before long be passed, such as the old navigation laws of England. They are quoting the navigation laws of Cromwell in the British House of Commons, and the navigation laws of Cromwell are to the effect that British goods must be carried in British bottoms. We should adopt some such system, because if we do we will

strengthen our trade and shipping, and we will be able to compete in the markets of the world with our surplus products. The sale of our surplus products and the increase of our foreign commerce will bring to the treasury of this country vast resources, and enable us to carry the burdens of the war very lightly.
The next subject I wish to discuss is the question of the returned soldier. The returned soldier will come back here filled with high hopes and courage, and he will be prepared to write the name of Canada commercially and industrially on the banners of the world just the same as he has done while fighting on the field of battle. It will be a great mistake for this House to continue idle discussion on economic topics or to consider proposals that will have the effect of thwarting the ambitions of these men upon their return home. They are the next generation, and in their hands will be placed the work of building up Canada. I am sure that there will be many hearty laughs when they read some of the speeches that have been delivered in this House during the war. Their eyes are opened. They realize what internationalism means to the world at large and particularly to their own country, and no doubt after the war is over we are going to have some form of union or of alliance between the nations which will be of some benefit to Canada.

With the
United States also?

I propose to speak
frankly to the House. I have discussed this question so far without taking up the question of the Imperial preference at all, because I feel that, possibly, the United States having once more become one of the great English-speaking nations, if any special favour were given to Canada that were not given to the United States, it might give offence. Hide-bound protectionist as I am, I would not be one of those who would say that it would be wrong for the United States to get an Imperial preference along with the British colonies. We are the same people, speaking the same language, and I think it is the brightest feature of the statesmanship of to-day that it can change its mind. The great men of to-day in the Old World, the men who are doing things, like Lloyd George, are the men who are changing their minds. A politician, or a man who has anything to do with political affairs, who sticks constantly to one line of thought, is not

the man who is cutting any figure in the world's history at the present time. The greatest men in England have cast aside the question of free trade. They have realized the necessity for a change. This world will not be the same again after the war, and if we receive an Imperial preference as one of the dominions of the Empire, and if the United States is desirous of coming in, there must be reciprocal advantages which we must all derive and it will not be wrong.
But, with reference to preferential tariff arrangements amongst the Allies, there is * a great deal of alarm amongst some so-called economists as to what is going to happen with regard to this question. It is all very simple. A four-column tariff is proposed by the Allies in opposition to the German proposals. The nature of the German proposals, as given expression to at their meeting in Vienna, is indicated clearly by this paper which I have here:
A secret conference of delegates of the Central European Economic Associations was held recently in Vienna, at which detailed proposals were formulated with reference to the questions of German, Austrian and Hungarian economic union. Under the leadership of the three presidents of the associations-Duke Ernst Gunther zu Schleswig-Holstein, Baron Plener, ex-Finance Minister, and Herr Wekerle, ex-President of the Council of Ministers, and with the participation of the prominent agricultural, industrial and commercial representatives of the three States, the following resolutions were passed:-
1.	Prior to peace negotiations being entered upon, the foundations are to be laid for the most comprehensive economic rapprochement between the German Empire and the two States of the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy.
2.	This economic rapprochement is to be brought about on the basis of reciprocal preferential treatment and must embrace as far as possible all aspects of economic life. Thus it is not only the unification of the customs system which is to come into consideration, but also the improvement and development of a reciprocal system of trade and traffic in the widest sense of the word.
3.	The basis of the customs part of the political reciprocal preferential treatment is to be-subject to full preservation of necessary protection of home production, including in exceptional cases even the raising of particular customs duties-that side by side with the reciprocally granted customs concessions, the free list of the customs tariffs is to be extended as much as possible and a periodic revision of the customs duties operative in the reciprocal trade undertaken, actuated by the spirit of rapprochement. Endeavours are likewise to be made to devise a unified customs tariff scheme and classification of commodities, as also customs administrative legislation which shall be as uniform as possible.
4.	It is to be a condition precedent of the customs political preferential treatment that- particularly in the treaties of peace-the principle shall hold that such preferential treatment shall not be accorded to other States on the basis of most-favoured-nation treatment.
5.	Commercial treaty negotiations with other States are to be carried out by the Allied Empires, subject to the preservation of their commercial political sovereign rights, in agreement with one another, and with mutual support and simultaneously; such treaties, too, being concluded simultaneously.
6.	All measures of a legislative or administrative technical character which appear necessary for the development of the production, trade, communication, and financial economy of their countries are to be carried out in the free economic territories with expedition in the sense of rapprochement and unification.
7.	The arrangements of the Allied Empires which eventuate in the sense of these proposals are to be made for a period which shall con * siderably exceed the duration hitherto customary for commercial treaties.
That is what they decided upon at Vienna. As tar as the Allies are concerned, the proposal has been made and it is considered almost virtually as an established principle, that there shall 'be a four-column tariff. Many people ask: How is a four-column tariff to be applied? Let me give an example. First, there will be a general tariff, which will apply to neutrals and to everybody. While that general tariff will apply to neutrals and to everybody, there will be a reduction of, say, 10 or 15 per cent in favour of the Allied nations. Then, between the British Colonies and the Empire there will be an Imperial preference of say, 33 per cent. That gives us three rungs of the ladder. The fourth rung will be a surtax of 25 per cent against Germany and the Central Powers. That is how it can be carried out, and it is very easy to carry it out. As far 'as Canada is concerned, It will be very easy, because we are accustomed to preferential treatment as between this country and Great Britain. There is no great disadvantage, but, on the other hand, there is a great advantage, because, when we go into an alliance of that kind, our raw materials, such as grain and the products of grain, will cut a large figure. If any man will take the trouble to study the economic questions and results consequent upon such an alliance he will ascertain thait the Allies, as constituted at the present time, contain within themselves all the elements that contribute to economic greatness. We are in a position to supply ourselves with all the grain that is necessary to meet the requirements of our peoples, and we will have 70,000,000 or 80,000,000 bushels to export to other countries, which will all work out to our advantage.
As a manufacturer, I realize the great advantage it is to the manufacturers of this country who 'are not making munitions to be able to export material to the four cor-

iiers of the globe. I am one of those manufacturers, because I am interested in a factory whose products are going into South America, South Africa, and other countries where German goods at a former period supplied the demand. .
It has proved a very profitable business. We are not alone in the enjoyment of that business; it is enjoyed also by the other manufacturers in this country. We enjoy that, and have had a taste of what foreign commerce means, and you have no idea what a great advantage it is in a factory to have an opportunity of disposing of surplus goods in a foreign country, instead of having to throw them on the markets of this country at reduced prices. It is a tremendous advantage, and it would be a tremendous advantage after the war if the manufacturers of Canada would take the place of Germany. Canadians are exceptionally able as factory employees; they are bright, intelligent, and become first class workmen, and Canada should be able to carry on foreign trade as well as Germany, the United States or any other nation. She should be able to carry it on better than the United States. We have a great advantage in cheap power; the white coal of Quebec and Ontario and the Maritime provinces is cheaper than coal, and enables small industries to be carried on in small buildings, upstairs, and in various places, in cities, towns and villages where formerly it was impossible to do any manufacturing without the installation of great steam plants. This will give us a great advantage, and if we get the advantage of a tariff from the Allies which will enaole us to displace Germany in many manufactures, the burden of taking care of returned soldiers, so far as this country is concerned, will be very light, and the country will go ahead by leaps and bounds.
I look forward to the period of the return cf our soldiers with a great deal of anxiety, i think that we in this House should make it Known to the people of Canada and to those who are likely to invest money in Canada, that, when the war is over, business will go on at the old stand in Canada, that the policy of destroying industry will not receive the endorsement, for instance, of the right hon. leader of the Opposition. It never did-
Never.

Because he was always
a good sound protectionist, in spite of the few free traders behind him. And it was [Mr. Currie.J
to his credit because, after all, any one familiar with conditions in this country, must know that we cannot all be farmers or tradesmen or lumbermen; somebody must carry on the manufactures of this country, and it is from the manufacturers of Canada and the skill of its workmen and textile workers that our future glory and greatness must come.
As one of the Canadians who did a little hit, perhaps, in the war and who has at heart the feelings of those men who are gallantly fighting for us at the front, I feel that the only hope for them is for Canada to adopt such a policy. You cannot expect all of our soldiers to come back and go on the farms. Many of them will be minus a leg or an arm, but they can still go into a factory and work as well as if they were whole in body and limb. But it would not be possible under any conditions for more than 40 per cent or 50 per cent of them to go on the farm. It is essential that we Should get behind them with the resources of the country. I am a great believer in the German system of state socialism, and I believe that we must develop a similar system; that we must have something to correspond particularly with their great system of rural credit banks, supplementing, not competing with, our present banking system. Ft is the rural credit banks of Germany, of Austria and of Hungary t/hai. are enabling the Central Powers to carry on the war to-day. The farmers of Germany, of Austria and of Hungary are buying the war bonds of those countries, and it is from them that the Central Powers have derived their financial strength and have been able to carry on the war. That is the great source of their economic strength.
I have no desire to enter into any lengthy discussion of the position of those gallant men who are fighting at the front, but I wish to say that I feel that- this House is behind them at the present moment and that the people of this country are behind them. It is only a few days since it was announced that we are to have some form of conscription in Canada. The Canadians at the front have had anxious moments. They have covered tnemselves with glory because, let me inform you, the battle of Vimy Ridge was a far greater battle, to my mind, and more decisive in the history of the world, than the battle of Waterloo. These men have covered themselves with glory; they have been decimated again and again, and it is necessary that we in Canada should keep up their strength.

I have always been a believer in a system of conscription, or as I like to call it universal national service-I hate the word "conscript" because I do not think it represents the proper feeling that should he in the bosom of everybody desirous of defending his country. The old Militia Act provided for a system of conscription. The right hon. leader of the Opposition in 1904 inserted a clause in the Militia Act -which enabled the soldiers, the militia men of this country, to be sent abroad for the defence of Canada as well as for service at home. The right hon. gentleman shakes his head; does he deny that? Yes? Well, I have no desire to discuss it, but section 69 of the Militia Act of 1902 was amended so that it now reads:
The Governor in Council may place the Militia, or any part thereof, on active service anywhere in Canadaand these are the words added in 1904:
-and also beyond Canada, for the defence thereof, at any time when it appears advisable to do so by reason of emergency.
Is that not correct? That means that the Governor General in Council at any moment when there is a war or invasion can declare that there is an emergency and call for a levy en masse of all the manhood of this country capable of bearing arms. That clause was put there because at the time of the South African war it was found that the Act did not permit a man to be called out under the Militia Act and sent to fight in South Africa. When the present war broke out, Canada was the only country in the Empire that had a conscription law on the statute book. I have read the clause, and if it is anything else than conscription I do not know what the English language means. The other countries of the Empire had what they ca'led the old Militia Act, which permitted a man to be called out for home defence only. The territorial law in England permitted a man to be called out only for home defence. The Australian law permitted a man to be called out only for the defence of Australia at home within her own borders. Premier Hughes had to put the question to the people whether they would have conscription or not.
A very good plan.

A very good plan,
but it is not in accordance with the principles of British Parliamentary government because prerogative rests with the Parliament, not with the people, as was shown
by the decision in British Columbia. Or if my hon. friend will read Walter Bagehot, who has studied the question fully, he will find that it is different from the American system under which prerogative comes from the people up.
If the Militia Act confers on the Government full authority to raise men by conscription, why has not the Government, of which my hon. friend is such a valiant supporter, put it into force?

I am not the Government and I do not understand why, because, so far as I am concerned as a member of the House, when I served in France I understood that I was serving under the Militia Act and I thought I was a militiaman and one of the members of the militia of Canada. Only when I returned home to Canada did I find that the overseas force fighting to-day was not raised under the Militia Act, but under the Defence of the Realm Act, or the Act that was passed when the war broke out. Further-I wish to speak frankly-it is a matter of considerable pain to those who are engaged in the war to know that they are npt a part of the militia of Canada. Officers who served overseas were notified that when the war ended and they returned to Canada, their rank would not be recognized under the Militia Act. The Order in Council which brought the Canadian Expeditionary Force into existence will be done away with simply by the passing of another Order in Council. I dp not know why the Militia Act was not applied, unless because of the feelings of some hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not understand why the Militia Act was not invoked in the first instance. The matter rested entirely in the hands of the late Minister pf Militia. All the requirements set forth in the Militia Act were present. The war was on; the militia was mobilized for war purposes; Parliament was called within ten days after the mobilization of the militia-but, strange to say, the Militia Act was not enforced. I do not wish to express any opinion in the matter; the fewer organizations we have in Canada dealing with military matters the better. I am sure that one army is enough for any country; in Canada we have several such organizations and, unfortunately, the most bitter enmity exists amongst some of them. The Expeditionary Force and the Permanent Force are not on the best pf terms. For instance, a colonel who is fighting to-day in the trenches is getting $6 a day, while a colonel who has

stayed at home, who has not even crossed the water, is drawing between $15 and $20. You can see, therefore, that anomalies have arisen, by the non-enforcement of the law. The law as it stands now is ail right. It provides for the organization of the troops, their enrollment, their being sent abroad.
It would be a disastrous thing for this country if we were to spend the summer discussing this Militia Act or the proposed conscription Bill. Whatever comes, let us support it, because the men at the front require support and assistance. To discuss this question at great length would, to my mind, be disastrous and a disgrace to the people who have sent such a magnificent army to the front. These men have distinguished themselves and are distinguishing themselves every day. It would be a great shame if their stars should be thrown into the sea as they came across, or into the waste-paper basket when they came home, and they were accorded no military recognition. Some amendment to the Act may be necessary before conscription can be fully carried out. But, instead of calling it conscription, let us call it universal national service. It would be disastrous in the extreme if the legislation enacted were such as to give ground for the opinion that the poor would have to serve, whereas the rich would escape, or that one part of the country would have to serve while another part would escape. Selective conscription was adopted in Great Britain because they wanted to omit Ireland from the scope of the legislation. I am sure that no part of this country wishes to escape its duty in connection with this war. Some people are mean enough to make insinuations about our good friends on the east side of the Ottawa river. I know differently, for I have seen them serve. The history of the French-Canadian people is such that they can very well be proud of it. They were not in any sense a conquered race when Canada was taken over. The French-Canadian militia never lowered its flag. When Canada was taken over the French-Canadian militia marched out of all the fortresses and positions with the full honours of war. They were fighting men, and, to my mind, their descendants are as brave, as national, and as strong for the Empire .as the men of that day were.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would remind the'hon. member that he is wandering somewhat far afield. I would ask him to confine his remarks more closely to the subject of the resolution.

Perhaps I am out of order in dealing with questions that will come up in the House later. However, I think this House should adopt ,a resolution showing the Allies that we are still steadfast in the war, showing our brave soldiers that we are still steadfast and that we are not going to desert them and leave them without reserves during such times of emergency as they went through on several occasipns this year.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at length on this question which has been so well discussed by my hon. friend (Mr. Currie). He has certainly taken advantage of the liberty that was given him by the Deputy Speaker to make his discussion of the matter fairly broad. I felt a little sorry that the Speaker, who sits in the Chair now, drew the circle a little closer because I am afraid it had the effect of cutting off the latter part of my hon. friend's speech. I am certain that the House must be deeply indebted to him for the wide field he has covered and for the arguments he has adduced.
The proposition which my hon. friend sets forth appeals, of course, to all of us. It is a matter in respect of which, as my hon. friend knows, a great deal has already been done by the Dominion Government, by the British Government, and by the Allies, in the way of preliminary investigations, conferences, discussions, arguments, and to a certain extent, acts. The economic conference which met in Paris last June was one of the developments of the feeling which had taken deep root in the minds of the Allies that certain considerations outside of the struggle for political hegemony were involved in the world wide contest; that beneath it and along with it there was an economic aspect. The conference, which was attended by the representatives of all the Allied countries, with the exception, I think, of Montenegro, devoted a week to the general discussion of the subject, came to certain conclusions which were immediately put into operation and came to an agreement upon certain principles which should be applied during the period of reconstruction, as well as during the time after the reconstruction period shall have passed and what might be called the permanent period of peace shall have been entered into. The action which had been taken by the Allies in respect of trade treatment of the enemy during the war was about

parallel to the course of action which was approved by the economic conference. Trade with the enemy, of course, is for* bidden., and we are to take advantage of every reasonable means of curtailing the enemy's trade expansion in every respect, and to push to the very utmost limit, consistent with fair treatment of neutral countries, the blockade which should restrict, restrain, and gradually diminish the power of the common enemy. The principle was also laid down that in the war, naval military, and economic, the Allies should in every possible way co-operate with each other, making common issues and, if necessary, even sacrificing in some respects individual preferences and even individual benefits if in that way the general Allied cause were made stronger as against the common enemy. Various methods were suggested for such co-operation. Great Britain, as being the greatest owner and director of mercantile transport has, in connection with the transport business of the world, carried out this principle of co-operation and help, even to the point of self-denial of her own purely economic or commercial interests. In financial matters the Allies have co-operated1 with each other, the strong aiding the weak, the weak taking advantage of the strong arm of the strong, each bearing the other's burdens. No definite length of time was set for the duration of the era of reconstruction-it might be two years, three years, or more-but with reference to what should take place in the war of economic and commercial treatment during that period, there was reached an agreement which has been ratified' by the Allied nations. That agreement was on this general basic principle:	you protect your
people with your arms, and with your blood and with sacrifices when you are in war; when war ceases, then you are to help each other in the work of reconstruction. The same principle of co-operation during the reconstruction period was affirmed in the resolutions of the Economic Conference, that is>
that the strong was to aid the weak, and that the different resources, eco-. nomie and otherwise, of the Allies as a whole, should be directed, not each one for its own special selfish benefit, but all for the general up-'building and reconstruction of the Allied peoples who have borne their part of the war and many of whom have been very severely harmed and damaged by the actual course of the war.

Did that principle imply no commercial intercourse
with the nations which at this moment are our enemies? I may Temind my right hon. friend that the action of the Paris Conference was interpreted) by the German Chancellor as implying enmity even after war, and he used it largely in order to prolong the war.

The interpretations of the German Chancellor are generally made with a view to strengthening the German cause with his own people, and I have no doubt he used that interpretation to the utmost limit. But if the Allied nations were at any time during the war to base their conduct upon possible interpretations of the German Chancellor, they would be reduced to inanity and weakness. What the Allied nations did do was to discuss the questions and come to conclusions as to what would be best for the Allied nations as a whole; and if the German Chancellor, in his appeals to his own people, chose to make capital out of their action, that was not the fault of the Allied nations, and they would have to take that disadvantage for the sake of the advantage on the other side.
In that Paris Conference, was any provision made for any new nation that was not at that time in the war, but that might become an ally-the United States is a case in point?

No provisions were made except to lay down principles to apply to all the Allies that were in the war then, and those principles would apply equally to countries that might come into the war later on. I do not say-and I hope my hon. friend has not the idea-that the actual details in the working out of the principles were considered. That was not part of the duty of the Economic Conference; its duty was to get at principles that might be carried out with the cohesion and co-operation of the Allied nations. From now on until we reach the period of re-construction, experts and men of affairs in all the different lines will work out the methods so as to apply these principles. With reference to a remark of my right hon. friend, I may say that while every one felt that the economic resources of the different Allies countries should be used for the reconstruction and benefit of the Allies, there was no disposition in that conference, nor was there a hint of it, that there should be anything like non-intercourse or enmity towards neutral powers. Nobody at that conference, so far as I have heard, wished to



do any harm commercially to neutral countries, and on two grounds:	Erst,
because friendship could be kept with all neutral countries, and, second, because the broad grounds of commercial development and progress would not be consistent with any attempt to make a close corporation amongst the Allied powers to the exclusion of trade with neutral powers. Therefore, I think that this criticism that has sometimes been levelled against the Economic Conference is one which has no foundation in fact.
As to what should take place after the period of reconstruction and in normal periods of peace, principles were laid down tentatively and carefully and along somewhat the same lines, especially as regards the retention of the same spirit of helpfulness and co-operation amongst those who had borne the burdens of the war and who had suffered its tremendous consequental damages. There again, however, there was no thought of the exclusion of trade with neutral powers. As' far as I have studied the discussions, I think there was the general apprehension that trade and commercial development was a world-wide phenomenon, and that it was neither possible nor beneficial that an attempt should be made to divide it up into air-tight compartments. At the same time, there was a strong adhesion to that idea of comradeship in trade, commerce, and development after the war which had been cemented in the comradeship of battle and bloodshed on the fields of conflict.
My hon. friend '(Mr. Currie) led us over a very wide field. As to the necessity for most things which he mentioned, I think we all agree. We want in the first place to do the very best we can, on his return to this country for the man who has gone out from our midst and has fought our battle against the German foe; I do not think on either side of the House there is the least difference of opinion in that respect. There may be difference as to the best methods of bringing that about, but as regards our treatment of the returned soldier in every state of health and condition -from the man who has 'been rendered incapable of future labour to the man who is partly incapacitated and has to be taught and helped, to the man in full possession of his physical vigour who takes up again his old profession or wishes to undertake some new branch of labour and of life-we all feel that we owe to these men a debt which must he paid, and it is for us who

have for the time being the management of affairs to make for them the best and wisest provision possible. That feeling which prevails in this country and m this House will, I believe, be appreciated, by the soldier. I do not think the soldier who comes back -after fighting our battles will feel that he ha6 simply to sit down and be nursed by the country bemuse of the service he has performed. He knows that he has performed gallant service, service of sacrifice and of great peril. That consciousness is with him, but he comes back to this country wdth the feeling that he wants to do hie part in the civil life of the country just as well and as nobly as he did his part in the military life of the country. He has a perfect right to ask for the sympathy and help of the country for which he has fought and suffered, and if that be given to him in reasonable measure we shall have little difficulty with him in hie effort to adapt and adjust himself to peaceful life. The returned soldier will have received much teaching and instruction that is not to be obtained in schools or in colleges, and which is only to be learned in that great drama of life in which he has played such a part. In certain essential elements he may therefore be a better citizen than without that experience and training. So I look to the adjustment of the returned soldier to the duties of civil and peaceful life as a matter of great importance, but not of such tremendous difficulty, if the country itself does its duty, as I believe it is determined to do, and if the soldier himself takes up his part in civil life as I believe the great bulk of our soldiers intend to. So much for the soldier settlement.
As regards trade and commerce-we want employment; our people need employment. There is no country in the world which has resources more ready at hand, more rich, more varied, and more widely distributed than has Canada, and if we can direct the capital and labour of our country in wise and reasonable ways to develop the great resources of this Dominion, there will be great things in store for us. But I am not one of those who believe-I think it would be wrong if we tried to believe-that we are going to float from the period of war into the period of peace without trouble, without great anxiety, without possibly a great deal of sacrifice and of difficulty. After a three-year period of dislocation, such an adjustment on so vast a scale is not an easy matter, and we cannot expect to go

through that operation on the flood time of prosperity. Prosperity will come afterward, in due time, but to my mind there will he a period in which difficulty, and lack of great prosperity will intervene and it is that period that will try the mettle and spirit of this country as much as the war is trying it to-day. You may put on tariffs until you are gray-haired and talk about them just as long and eloquently as you choose, but there are only two ways, either by internal commerce or by external commerce, in which this country can march to prosperity on the line of the development of its great natural resources, and that is along the line of wise laws, tariff and otherwise. We must have legislation to suit the time and the occasion. But even if we should have the best tariff legislation possible, we still need an accordant working of labour and capital on the basis of equal advantage to each, taking the circumstances into account, and without either one or the other wishing to gobble up the larger share. Labour and capital working together wisely, intelligently, and sympathetically is one thing essential in this country, and it will be necessary in all countries when the war ceases. Then it cannot be too often said that we cannot compete in the home field in this country with the man from outside unless we can make goods as efficiently, as cheaply, and as tastefully as our competitor, and we certainly cannot get into the foreign market unless we can do the same thing there. Therefore, we have got to have a working body which has received the best education possible on the lines of practical work and technical education and all that kind of adaptation of labour to the spirit of the time and to the object to be produced which is going to be one of the great factors of future development and future prosperity. So in these respects we have in the first place to get the wisest legislation possible. Then we .have to get the closest co-operation between capital and labour. Then we have to get the most intelligent and best trained artisans and workers in the producing classes that we possibly can.
That is the object, I think, that my hon. friend has in view. His plan is to be carried out, in the first place in Canada for the development of Canada; in the second place in the Empire, for the development of the Empire as a whole; and in the third and fourth places for those outside of our own family who have the distinct relationship of ally or of neutral, with the bond of sympathy and co-operation, greater with
101 i
the former than with the latter, as is natural and right. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Currie) is to be congratulated upon bringing this matter forward and treating it, as he has, so broadly and so well. The Government has no objection at all to the passage of the resolution. In fact, the Government has been working along in consonance with the Overseas Dominions and the British Government and, to a certain extent, with the Allies, for the years of the war, and it proposes to work along the same lines in the years of peace that are to come.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) tells us that the Government has no objection to the passage of this resolution. I think I can safely say that no one on this side has any objection to U. But it seems to me it is altogether uncalled for; it declares for exactly what we have been doing all along. Can the hon. member for North Siincoe (Mr. Currie) point to any member of this House, either on this side or on his own side, who is not desirous of doing the best he can on lines indicated in the resolution? I do not complain of the resolution, but I do complain that the hon. gentleman has taken advantage of the moving of this resolution to make a most bitter partisan attack on members of this side, and has practically said that we have been sniping under a flag of truce. If any members of this House have been guilty of that sort of thing, I think the hon. member (Mr. Currie) himself is as guilty as any of the rest. Not very long ago there was a bye-election in Ontario, and of all the bitter partisan utterances I ever read, I think his speeches in that campaign were about the worst. This was during the war, and I was told-I do not state it as a fact-that he was in uniform when he made those speeches. I can hardly think it true, and I expect him to say that it is not true.
It is not true. It is like the rest of the lies they told about that campaign.

But the hon. gentleman will not deny his own speeches, for I read reports of them in newspapers that support the Government. I had not intended to speak on this resolution, but as the hon. gentleman has selected some members on this side, myself included, as the objects of attack, I feel called upon to take part in

the debate. The hon. member says that we are endeavouring to shut up the manufactories of this country. I never in my life advocated a policy to the detriment of our manufacturers, nor do I wish to hurt any manufacturer. The policy that I advocate is one which will give the manu-
5	p.m. facturer less tariff protection than he has now, when he has two or three times what he needs. But it will bring about such a condition of affairs that the workingmen, the farmers, and the consumers generally, will have money in their pockets and will be able to buy the goods that the manufacturer makes. And what better can the manufacturer ask? Can he expect to prosper under a policy that does not tend to prosperity of the common people? In my opinion, what the manufacturer needs is a market. At present, he has a market abroad, owing to special conditions that will end with the war. Why should it be said that one who wishes to reduce the tariff seeks to injure the manufacturers? Prior to 1896 the old Conservative Government made reductions in the tariff. Did that close up any manufactories? My hon. friend (Mr. Currie) is a manufacturer; can he point out a case where putting an article on the free list that previously had been subject to duty closed up a factory? I was talking to a manufacturer the other day, and in the course of the conversation he mentioned some lines of his production on which there were high protective duties. But as to these he complained of lack of business. Incidentally, he mentioned one class of goods that he was manufacturing, which is on the free list, but in the production of this line he was making better money than in any other line. I was talking to another manufacturer about a month ago-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Turriff) has had an opportunity, of which he has taken advantage, to deny the imputations of the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie). Having done so, I hope he will not enter upon a discussion of a subject that is not covered by the resolution.

I bow to your Tuling, of course, Mr. Speaker. But the hon. member (Mr. Currie) went faT afield, and with the consent of the hon. member who was then acting as Speaker, and I think it only reasonable that I should be allowed to answer some of the statements he made

against hoh. members on this side, myself in particular.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: But the hon. member (Mr. Turriff) has already given denial to those statements.

With your permission,
Mr. Speaker, I would remark that the hon. member (Mr. Turriff) brought it upon himself by an interruption.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, I probably have said enough on the point with which I am dealing. I take up another statement of the hon. member which no doubt comes within the terms of his resolution. He talks of preparedness and says that it was because of our unpreparedness and that of Great Britain that this war was brought on. Did preparedness ever keep any country out of waT?
I might point to the Morocco incident, England was ready for war then, and Germany was not.

Germany has been ready for war for the last twenty-five years, and has been preparing all the time. It was the preparedness of many nations for war that brought on the war. The hon. member went on to speak of those who were opposed to preparedness and said they should be put in the asylum. Well, Mr. Speaker, we do not treat the advocates of preparedness in that way; we make colonels of them. Instead of going to Britain for his ideas and ideals, the hon. member prefers to go to Germany, and all afternoon he has held up Germany as the nation that we should copy after. I do not think my hon. friend will get much backing up either on this side of the House or his own when he proposes that we should go to Germany for our model in -carrying on the civilization or business of the world. Britain is good enough for me. With her mistaken policy of free trade in everything practically excepting liquors, tobacco and a few luxuries, she is able to conduct the big end of this war and to loan money by hundreds of millions of pounds to all the Allies, and all the countries borrowing from her are high protectionist countries. That, I think, is a sufficient answer to that part of his argument.
My hon. friend said that Canada should be the paper-maker of the world. Perhaps she should, but I can assure my hon. friend that as long as Canada has a high protective tariff on everything that practically goes into the making of paper, whether she makes the paper down on the Atlantic coast

or up in the central portion of Canada, or out on the Pacific coast, she will not be the paper-maker of the world. By high protection you make the cost of machinery, wages and the feeding and clothing of the people so high that you cannot manufacture paper or anything else cheaply enough to enable you to compete with the other countries of the world that make paper under better conditions and with lower rates of freight.
Another idea that my hon. friend advocated as one which was going to solve all our difficulties was that we should take over the railways and' carry manufactured goods from the manufacturers to the seaports at the same rate of freight for 2,000 or 3,000 miles as was charged for 25 miles. What would the people, who have to pay for keeping these roads up, think of carrying raw material from Montreal to Edmonton there to be manufactured and then shipped back to Montreal to be exported at the same rate of freight that the manufacturers in Ottawa paid to ship goods to Montreal? To my mind the suggestion is very, very unreasonable. It is not feasible at all, and bad and all as the railway situation may be in Canada, if my hon. friend undertook hr remedy it in that manner, it would be just out of the frying pan into the fire, because he would make the situation much woree. There are some things you cannot do to advantage in the West. The manufacturing of many lines of goods is amongst those things that cannot be done to advantage. We can grow almost all kinds of farm produce to advantage. Let the manufacturing be done largely in the east under a proper tariff, not a protective tariff, but a revenue tariff. The tariff on, many lines now is such that we do not get any revenue out of it. But, I am afraid I will get on the wrong side of your ruling, again, Mr. Speaker, so that I will not go any farther on that subject.
My hon. friend stated that he was pleased to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) on having set apart money for the building of ships in Canada. I think he was mistaken there. I listened very carefully to the Minister of Finance in all the speeches he has made in connection with the matter and I do not think I heard him say that he had set aside one dollar of Canadian money for the building of ships. Hon members on this side of the House have advocated for the last two' years that the Government should do something in connection with the building of ships, but they have not done so and the
Minister of Finance did not say, as far as I understood him, that one dollar of Canadian money was being placed to the Imperial Munitions Board for the purpose of building ships. It is all British money that is being handled in that way.
There is just one other item that I wish to touch on before I sit down. The hon. member for North Simcoe made the statement that this Government was paying lieutenant-colonels-or colonels-I forget which-who were not at the war and who were not going to the war, from $15 to $20 a day, and that colonels who are bearing the brunt of the battle in the trenches are getting $6 a day. If that statement is correct it is the most scandalous charge I ever heard made against the Government since the House met. Why should a colonel in Canada get from $15 to $20 a day who is taking no risk, and who is going around with his frills and feathers while the man who has the courage of his convictions and who goes to the front and faces the enemy is getting $6 a day? If that is the case, Mr. Speaker, and I suppose it must be, because I imagine my hon. friend knows what he is talking about, there is an explanation coming from the Government, an explanation to the people of Canada, and there is more than an explanation, there is action coming from the Government that will put a stop and put a stop at once to that state of affairs. The fighting colonel gets $6 a day and the tea-party colonel gets $15 a day, to put it at the lowest figure. I am just drawing the attention of the Government to it. I do not know anything about it but I take the statement made by the hon. member and I say that if it is correct then there is action coming from the Government and that quickly. The Minister of Militia (Sir Edward Kemp) is out of the House at present or I would ask him if the statement is correct. We will expect the Government to make some statement in that connection and, if conditions exist, such as have been stated to exist, action must be taken and taken promptly to bring about a better state of affairs. If there is any advantage to be given it should be given to the man who is at the front and not to the man at home. My hon. friend the Parliamentary Secretary for the Department of Militia and Defence (Mr. McCurdy) is here and he will probably be able to give the information.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would suggest that my hon. friend put his question on the Order Paper.

I have brought the matter to the attention of the Government, and if they are not able to answer it, or do not care to answer it, why, it is their responsibility. There is one other matter that my hon. friend dealt with, that I will not deal with to-day, and that is in connection with the returned soldiers. That is a wide matter and one that I intend to have something to say about at the proper time. But as there will be many other opportunities for the discussion of that question I will pass it over to-day, and I will not deal further with the remarks of the hon. member for North Simcoe than to emphasize that he was absolutely mistaken when he stated that I was in favour of the closing of any manufactory of any kind in Canada.
Motion agreed to.

On the proposed motion of Mr. Pugsley:
That, whereas, in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan anti Alberta, the provincial franchise has been granted to women by legislative enactment, and in British Columbia the electors have voted in favour of similar legislation ;
Whereas it is provided in the Dominion Election Act that persons entitled to vote for Members of a Provincial Legislature shall also be entitled to vote for Members of Parliament, but in respect to Alberta and Saskatchewan

alone of all the provinces of Canada-it is provided that only males shall be entitled to vote for Members of the Federal Parliament, thus creating an anomalous situation as between the provinces, which should be removed :
Whereas during the present 'Umpire struggle the women of Canada have shown a most intelligent and patriotic interest in, and an unselfish devotion to, the welfare of the State;
And whereas It seems hut just and right that they should he given a voice in the direction of its affairs:
In the opinion of this House it is desirable that provision he made either to grant to women who are qualified to vote for Members of a Provincial Legislature, the right also to vote for Members of the Dominion Parliament, or to grant to women throughout the Dominion the right to vote for Members of Parliament, subject to such provisions and limitations as may seem reasonable to Parliament.
Dropped.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. BURNHAM (West Peterborough) moved:
subsubtopic: MOTION AS TO THE SCALE OF PENSIONS,
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable that the Government should fully realize that this House, while approving largely its past efforts to provide fully and amply for returned soldiers, would favour legislation providing for those who have fought for their country so that they may not he compelled to resort to canvassing and other unsuitable measures to eke out a livelihood which should be provided by the country for those practically disabled and unable to find suitable employment ; and that generally it be understood by the Government that this matter is one for immediate and complete consideration; and further that pensions and other provisions on behalf of soldiers and their families should automatically rise or fluctuate as prices do, so that the amounts thereof be not curtailed or decreased as at present to the detriment of those for whom Canada is under every obligation to provide.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my object in putting this resolution on the Order Paper was manifestly to give the House an opportunity of expressing its opinion up to date concerning a matter of the first importance. It will be remembered that last year, when the Pension Bill was foreshadowed, I put a resolution on the Order Paper of the same tenor as this. On investigating the Bill last year I found no less than 26 cardinal objections to it, and I did myself the honour of sending to some members of the House, notably the members of the Government and the right hon. leader of the opposition, a schedule of these, in order that they might be taken into consideration. However, later on a special committee was appointed to consider the question, and as I presumed it would deal with all the objections that I as well as others had made, I took no further practical interest in the matter with regard to the resolution itself. But I find that the pension scheme which was then brought down has a great many vulnerable points in it, of so serious a character that unquestionably the whole subject should be thrown open for discussion.
I have intimated in my resolution that there are three main divisions for reconsideration. One is that the men are not properly provided for; in other words, that

the pension list is not sufficiently munificent. Another is with regard to the finding of suitable employment for those who will be out of employment; and the third is with regard to the fluctuation of prices, since a stated pension is manifestly greater or less according to the fluctuation of the prices which it is intended to meet. I am aware that the Government is actuated by a desire to deal with soldiers most generously. I understand that a Pension Bill is coming down that will be a great improvement on anything we have had before. I have no doubt of that. But it may be possible that we shall have some suggestions to make to-day that may help in a case like this, and we cannot afford to omit anything that may be of the least advantage to the soldier and his dependents.
The true basis of a pension scheme in a democratic country like Canada should be equality; that is, that there should be really no distinction between officers and men. The spirit of the pension scheme as outlined in this memorandum which was served upon us all recently would indicate, in fact it specifically states, that the pension shall have no reference to the previous occupation of the soldier. Well, it should have no reference to the subsequent occupation of the soldier. I freely admit my appreciation of discipline and of that halo of distinction that must necessarily attach to an officer in authority over a large body of men, who, like a magistrate, or like you, Mr. Speaker, is more or less clothed in a distinction which is perhaps, though very fitting, nevertheless somewhat artificial. I could therefore understand that when a colonel or any such officer is in the actual course of his employment he should have a larger salary, a larger pay, a larger wage, than a soldier. But when he comes out of the fight he should not have a larger pay. I can find no reason why he should. There is no reason why by reason of any distinction that he has acquired or any service that he has rendered or not rendered he or any member of his family should have a larger pay than any other retired soldier. If this House, or the country desires to reward him particularly it is open to the House to move that he should have a larger sum of money placed to his credit or some other distinction conferred upon him. It is open to the Government or to the authorities to decorate him with various medals. Those are the things provided for that purpose. But when we come down to a simple commercial consideration of the question,
he has no title to richer food, better apartments, finer accommodations and generally better, support by the country than any other man who has done his duty, because I am convinced that a sense of duty, a sense of self sacrifice, is the highest qualification for merit. Absolutely we are not civilized until we reach that stage. If any other thing, such as the acquirement of property or the leverage that a large income may give, is to be the climax of our demo- 1 cratic distinction, then all I have to say is that we have not reached that peculiar and subtle form of the true spirit of democracy which means that sacrifice is far greater than property. Therefore I would urge that this feature of the matter should be very carefully considered. I may say in general terms that the soldier and his family should be, so far as necessary, even to the straining of a point, wards, of the nation. Therefore I give utterance to my absolute dislike of the provision that after a boy is 15 years of age and a girl 17 there should be no further payment of pension on his or her account. That is preposterous; it is absolutely improper. Wards in chancery are taken care of until they are 21, being the children of the court until they attain that age. It has never Ibeen suggested that a boy is of age when he is 15 or a girl when she is 17. We should try to find out, not how little we can do, but how much we can do without offending the soldier and his family. Let us be ever ready to help.
Another thing, I must confess, appears to me to be extraordinary. When a man is discharged from the Expeditionary Force he gets 15 days' pay and then he goes into the domain or the zone of the province, which is supposed to find him employment. I say that that is wrong. This man is taken out of the life of the country, in which, perhaps, he was earning a very comfortable salary. He may have been a plumber, a coal dealer, a man of that description, making money, hand over fist. He dropped i!t all, dropped his prospects, dislocated his whole domestic system and went abroad to fight. Having done these things, he is told, when he comes back: we will give you 15 days' notice, to enable you to get into your proper sphere of civil life. That is my understanding of the procedure, >and I certainly think it is improper.

subsubtopic: MOTION AS TO THE SCALE OF PENSIONS,
speechtext: I understand the hon. gentleman's reference; I will return to it in a few moments. The present pensions for the men are, I confidently assert, away below what they ought to Ibe, especially in view of the fact that when the men set out prices were 50 per cent lower than they are now. Indeed, the necessities of life have advanced, roundly speaking, 100 per cent; yet the pensions remain the same. If we were paying a salary, or a wage, well and good. Then we might say caveat emptor-let the man who makes the contract look after himself. But it is not so. We have said to the soldier: Go and fight for us; we will look after you; do not worry about that. And the way we look after him is to give him a pension which is now only half what it was when the pension list was first made out; yet we do not purpose increasing it in any way. And, strange to say, a man who is totally disabled gets $480 a year while his wife gets nothing. His children are provided for, but his wife gets nothing, on the principle, I assume, that man and wife are one, and therefore the wife is not entitled to anything. Or it may be that it, is supposed that she would like to take in washing or something of that kind, doing something towards the support of the family. I do not endorse that view. I think that single men should be provided for on one scale and married men on another, and certainly the wife should not be ignored.
